subject: Estimating N when groups are used

messages.author: 3908a2da5354fc44
messages.subject: Estimating N when groups are used
parts:
I am estimating bobcat abundance on an island from collection of bobcat
scat with individuals identified via genetic analysis. My questions are
whether I have constructed a reasonable model and about interpretation
of output.

I have analyzed the data from transects where each transect is divided
into 200 m segments and we assume the center of each segment is a count
detector. Effort is how many times a transect segment was searched
(binary.usage=FALSE). This is how I read in the data and code to run the
best model:

read.capthist("CUIS2018caploc.txt","CUIStrapID2018.txt",
detector="count",  covnames=c("sex"), binary.usage=FALSE)
secr.fit(capthist=bobcat, groups=c("sex"), model=list(D~1, a0~1,
sigma~g), mask=areaextent, buffer = 50, method="Nelder-Mead")

N animals       :  21 (F=14, M=7)
N detections    :  62
N occasions     :  1
Count model     :  Poisson
Mask area       :  4985 ha

Model           :  D~1 a0~1 sigma~g
Fixed (real)    :  none
Detection fn    :  halfnormal
Distribution    :  poisson
N parameters    :  4

I used the parameterization of Efford and Mowat (2014) because that
seems appropriate given that males should have larger home ranges.

When I use region.N I get very different estimates for E.N and R.N

> region.N(bobcat.fit.final, region = boundary, RN.method="MSPE")
        estimate    SE.estimate      lcl            ucl            n
E.N 16.45107    3.687841       10.65894 25.39067 21
R.N 37.45107    5.451656       29.73842 51.97102 21

and it appears that E.N is the estimate for only 1 sex.

So my initial questions are:

1. Am I correct that E.N only represents abundance for 1 sex (even
though the model specifies D~1 with 2 groups [group=sex])? Could R.N
represent both males and females?
2. From what I have been able to find online, if E.N and R.N differ
there is a "problem." Any insights into what that might be for my
situation? Does it relate to the fact that I have an island where there
truly are no bobcats outside the mask? Perhaps how I have set up the
analysis, given that this is an island, is the problem?
3. Since region.N does not appear to be set up for groups, I guess I
simply should calculate N outside of secr?

Thanks for any suggestions/insights,

Duane

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Estimating N when groups are used
parts:
Hi Duane

region.N() has never worked with groups (this is mentioned deep in the help; I haven't got around to fixing that).
But don't give up. There are many ways allowing for sex without using groups. For a simple example
library(secr)
mask <- make.mask(traps(ovenCH[[1]]), buffer = 300, nx = 32)
fit2 <- secr.fit(ovenCH[[1]], CL = TRUE, model = sigma~Sex, mask = mask, trace = FALSE) # or
fit3 <- secr.fit(ovenCH[[1]], model = sigma~h2, hcov = 'Sex', mask = mask, trace = FALSE)
region.N(fit2)
region.N(fit3)

The estimate of total density doesn't change. However, there is still a disconcerting difference between E.N and R.N, and I can't put my finger on why that is (from memory Eric Howe addressed this a long time back). I'll get back to you when I've explored further.

I think there are a couple of rough edges in your code. (i) no need to specify buffer if you specify a mask, (ii) I wonder if you really need a different boundary for region.N, rather than relying on the original mask, and (iii) you (probably unintentionally) fitted a model with 50:50 sex ratio (D~1); this is avoided in the code above.

Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Estimating N when groups are used
parts:
It seems that a discrepancy between E.N and R.N arises in 'secr' with models that include individual variation in detection (both my earlier examples fit2 and fit3 are of this type). The code only considered the detection probability (and effective sampling area esa) of the first animal. The problem has been there forever. The sensible path is to take the harmonic mean of the individual esa as is done when computing H-T estimates of density in derived(). I have made this 1-line change to the internal function sumDpdot that is called by region.N() and re-built the package. This passes routine checks but won't be on CRAN until later in September (I'm traveling and CRAN incoming has a long maintenance shut down in early Sept.). Meantime you can access it at https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.7.zip (Windows binary) or https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.7.tar.gz (source).

Repeating the earlier examples
region.N(fit2)
#     estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n
# E.N 81.20962    30.82438 39.56661 166.6810 20
# R.N 81.20962    29.47767 45.00768 169.8187 20
region.N(fit3)
#     estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n
# E.N 81.21036    31.97651 38.58809 170.9108 20
# R.N 81.21037    30.68040 44.20184 174.8109 20

E.N and R.N now agree.

I'm guilty of not attending to parts of 'secr' that never much excited me (N-hat and telemetry) - I'm sorry if this has tripped people up.

Murray
